back: v = lim(dt->0) of Dx/Dt = dx/dt. It is the rate of change of position with respect to time at that instant — the slope of the tangent to the x-t curve at that instant.
Instantaneous speed always equals |instantaneous velocity|. But over a finite interval, average speed (path length / time) >= |average velocity|.
For x = 0.08t³, shrinking Dt centring t = 4 s pushes Dx/Dt towards 3.84 m s⁻¹ = dx/dt at t = 4 s.
a = (v₂ − v₁)/(t₂ − t₁) = Dv/Dt. SI unit m s⁻². On a v-t plot it is the slope of the chord joining the two points.
a = lim(Dt->0) Dv/Dt = dv/dt — the slope of the tangent to the v-t curve at the given instant.
Galileo found dv/dt is constant for all free-falling objects, while dv/dx decreases with distance. Hence acceleration is the time rate of change of velocity.
Area between t₁ and t₂ equals the displacement over that interval — because v dt = dx. For constant u over 0 to T the area is the rectangle uT.
v = v₀ + at; x = v₀t + ½at²; v² = v₀² + 2ax. Valid only for constant acceleration; general forms replace x by x − x₀.
x = v̄ t with v̄ = (v₀ + v)/2 — valid only for constant acceleration. The arithmetic average of initial and final velocities.
Eliminate t between v = v₀ + at and x = v₀t + ½at² (or via the v-t area with v − v₀ = at).

front: Ball thrown up from 25 m: rise height and total time
back: v₀ = 20 m s⁻¹, g = 10 m s⁻²: rise = v₀²/2g = 20 m. Total time = 5 s (2 s up + 3 s down from 45 m, or the single quadratic 5t² − 20t − 25 = 0).

front: Why is the 'single equation' method better?
back: Under constant acceleration one correctly-signed equation handles the whole motion — no need to split and track the path. Solving 0 = 25 + 20t − 5t² gives t = 5 s directly.
a = −g = −9.8 m s⁻²; v = −9.8t; y = −4.9t²; v² = −19.6y. The a-t graph is a horizontal line, v-t a straight line of slope −g, y-t a downward parabola.
A body falling from rest traverses 1, 3, 5, 7, … units of distance in successive equal time intervals — because positions go as 1, 4, 9, 16, ….
d_s = v₀²/(2a). Proportional to the square of the initial velocity — doubling speed quadruples the stopping distance.
t_r = sqrt(2d/g) where d is the distance the dropped ruler falls. For d = 21.0 cm, t_r ≈ 0.207 s ≈ 0.2 s.
A ball at its highest point has v = 0 but a = g. Momentary rest does not imply vanishing acceleration.

front: Sign of acceleration vs speeding up
back: The sign of a alone tells nothing about speeding/slowing — it depends on the axis choice. Under gravity (upward positive) a falling particle has negative a yet speeds up; a rising particle has negative a yet slows down.
Treat a body as a point object when its size is much smaller than the distance it moves in the interval of interest — valid for a carriage between stations, not for a tumbling beaker.
Sharp kinks mean the function is not differentiable there. Realistically acceleration and velocity change continuously, so graphs are always smooth.
Bullet ground speed = 150 + 8.33 ≈ 158.3 m s⁻¹; relative to the car at 53.3 m s⁻¹ → impact speed ≈ 105 m s⁻¹.

front: Which kinematic-equation quantities can be negative?
back: All of them — displacement, velocity, acceleration, even time in some contexts. Substitute with proper signs after choosing the axis.
Straight line → zero acceleration; curving upward with positive a, downward with negative a; a parabola segment signals constant non-zero acceleration — the motion is still one-dimensional.
